text: To live up to the hype
To put somewhere on the map
I do think it is overrated, and I say that with affection.
It is precisely because it is run-down that it still has character.
The very fact that nobody photographs it is the point.
The old town is every bit as good as the guidebooks say.
I have made a career out of unfashionable cities, and I will tell you the pattern. Everybody who dislikes one has spent two days in it, both of them in the centre.
I do recognise that. Although in fairness, two days in the centre is what most people get.
It is, and the centre is usually the worst part. It is teeming with visitors, the prices are absurd, and the people who actually live there left it years ago.
So what would you send somebody to see instead? Not a hidden gem from a guidebook — something real.
A market at seven in the morning, and then a residential street forty minutes out. The very fact that nothing is happening there is what you are looking at.
That is a hard sell to somebody with two days.
It is. And it is precisely because it is a hard sell that the cities stay misunderstood. A place that photographs badly is assumed to be soulless, which is a category error.
Every bit as much a category error as assuming that a photogenic one has substance.
It is nothing like as difficult as people tell you.
Far and away the better hour is the market at seven.

Start at the market, and start at seven, because by ten it is a different place and by noon it is a photograph. Walk east from there, down the street that looks like nothing, past the two closed shops, and keep going for about fifteen minutes. You will come out at the cathedral square. Give it ten minutes. It is overrated, everybody who comes here sees it first, and it will tell you nothing you cannot get from a postcard. Then take the number four bus north for twenty stops. Get off when the buildings stop being interesting. Walk one residential street, slowly, and look at the balconies. That is the city. Nothing is happening there, and the fact that nothing is happening is exactly what you came to see.

Let me put the other side, and let me start by conceding most of it. Walkable cities are pleasant. The evidence on health, on street life, on the simple question of whether anybody talks to anybody, is real and I do not dispute it. My objection is narrower. In practice, in city after city, the schemes that make a district walkable also make it expensive, and within a decade the people the policy was written for cannot afford to live there. They now commute in, by car, from somewhere with no pavements at all. And here is the part that troubles me most. Those people are never in the room when the plan is drawn. The consultation happens where the residents are, and the residents of tomorrow are somewhere else entirely.
